title: Perioperative anesthetic management of perforated appendicitis in a pregnant patient with severe pulmonary hypertension: a rare case report
authors: Tesfaye Asefa Hordofa; Dinku Tsegaye Urji; Kelil Musa Nerso; ﻿Tajera Tageza Ilala
abstract: Abstract Background The incidence of severe pulmonary hypertension associated with a valvular heart disease in pregnancy is very rare. This patient may have presented with different defects like Eisenmneger syndrome, systematic- to-pulmonary shunts, and other defects. This case report contributes to the existing literature by providing insight into the perioperative anesthetic management of early first - trimester pregnant patient with severe pulmonary hypertension and mixed valvular heart disease who presented with perforated appendicitis. Case presentation We report a 26-year-old woman in early pregnancy presenting with abdominal pain diagnosed as perforated appendicitis. She had a history of palpitations, shortness of breath, orthopnea, fatigue, and chest pain at exertion prior to this complaint. She had a grade II holosystolic murmur at the second intercostal space and apex but no radiating on cardiac examination. Echocardiography revealed severe pulmonary hypertension (estimated pulmonary artery pressure 91 mmHg) with mixed valvular heart disease (moderate mitral stenosis, severe mitral regurgitation, mild aortic regurgitation, and mild-to-moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Conclusion General anesthesia effectively managed severe pulmonary hypertension and mixed valvular heart disease using etomidate (0.3 mg/kg), balanced with opioids, and minimizing airway stimulation with 1% lidocaine and midazolam before intubation.

title: Advancing arrhythmia diagnostics in cardiology and cardio-oncology - from bench to bedside
authors: Justin Anh-Kiet Phan
journal: UNSWorks (University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia)
abstract: Drug-induced long QT syndrome and atrial fibrillation are common arrhythmias encountered in the clinical care of patients with cancer. Improvements in the detection of these arrhythmias and a better understanding of pro-arrhythmic states may result in an improved ability to risk stratify and screen for arrhythmic toxicity in cancer patients. We sought to better understand the risk of drug-induced long QT syndrome in patients undergoing targeted therapy combinations in breast cancer, to detect atrial fibrillation using a machine-learning model that utilised electrocardiographic (ECG) images and to improve the arrhythmia discrimination potential in patients undergoing extended ECG monitoring with implantable cardiac monitors (ICMs). Firstly, we used a high-throughput patch clamp electrophysiology (Syncropatch, Nanion) to determine the acute effects of various breast cancer therapies (ribociclib, palbociclib, letrozole, fulvestrant, alpelisib and buparlisib) on the human ether-a-gogo (hERG) potassium ion channel, the commonest mechanism for drug-induced long QT syndrome. We found that the hERG half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) using our approach differed significantly from those published in regulatory submissions. Furthermore, when correcting for the clinical maximum serum concentration (Cmax), we were able to predict the clinically observed QT prolonging effects of these medications with more accuracy than those based on the data in the regulatory submissions. Secondly, we developed an ensemble of four neural networks to perform classification of atrial fibrillation on ECG images. Our ensemble of neural networks classified atrial fibrillation with similar performance to a neural network that utilised the raw digital signals. Furthermore, we found that changing ECG layout significantly affected the performance of our neural network, but this effect was ameliorated if the training dataset incorporated an equal amount of each ECG format. Finally, we sought to assess the effect of ICM implant location on P wave sensing in patients undergoing extended ECG monitoring with ICMs. This is an important metric for arrhythmia discrimination, especially for the detection of atrial fibrillation, which is usually characterised by a lack of distinct P waves. We found that insertion of ICMs in the third left intercostal space, as compared to the manufacturer-recommended fourth intercostal space, resulting in a larger P wave amplitude, but with similar QRS amplitude. Our findings have implications for drug development in oncology as well as providing the underpinnings for the development of clinical tools that could be implemented into clinical care of cancer patients.

title: Congestive heart failure and other cardiac adverse events after intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Michael Balas; Andrew Mihalache; Aaditeya Jhaveri; Shayaan Kaleem; Marko M Popovic; Peter J. Kertes; Rajeev H Muni
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate congestive heart failure (CHF) and other cardiac adverse events (AEs) after intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy for retinal vascular disease and compare risks across agents. DESIGN: A systematic review and meta-analysis. METHODS: Registered review (PROSPERO CRD42022302658) searched Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from January 2005 to February 2024 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for neovascular age-related macular degeneration, diabetic macular edema, or retinal vein occlusion. Eligible trials compared an anti-VEGF agent with sham or another anti-VEGF agent and reported CHF (primary outcome) or other cardiac AEs (secondary outcomes: arrhythmias, heart failure/cardiomyopathy, inflammatory heart disease, ischemic heart disease, or valvular heart disease). Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, certainty with GRADE, and random-effects models generated risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: Fourteen reports describing 20 trials (11,803 eyes; mean age 71 ± 12 years; 53% female) were included. CHF was uncommon overall: aflibercept 2.0% (84/4172), ranibizumab 2.2% (25/1158), faricimab 2.3% (44/1926), brolucizumab 2.5% (40/1612), and sham 3.8% (20/524). Ranibizumab did not differ from sham for CHF (RR = 1.53, 95% CI 0.46-5.06), whereas aflibercept was associated with higher CHF risk versus sham in 2 trials (RR = 2.08, 95% CI: 1.03-4.23). No significant CHF differences were detected between aflibercept and brolucizumab, faricimab, or ranibizumab. Other cardiac events were similar across agents. CONCLUSIONS: CHF and other AEs after intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy were uncommon in RCTs and comparable across agents. The aflibercept-sham CHF signal was based on limited evidence and should be interpreted cautiously.

title: EMERGENCY MEDICINE High-Yield Triage Study Guide v1.0
authors: Joshua Moen
abstract: This educational guide applies a top-down, layered approach to emergency medicine learning. It begins with high-yield, testable facts for rapid retrieval, then progressively moves into clinical context, anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology, diagnostic reasoning, and management. This structure distinguishes performance at the surface level from deeper understanding: mastery of examination facts does not necessarily demonstrate mastery of the mechanisms beneath them. Designed for health-professions learners preparing for course examinations, PANCE, USMLE, and OSCE-style assessments.

title: Association between sleep quality and self-care in patients with heart failure: a cross‑sectional study
authors: Leili Valizadeh; Zahra Jafari Loghman; Alireza Mirzaei; Reza Nemati Vakilabad; Mehraban Shahmari
abstract: Sleep quality is a critical but understudied factor in heart failure (HF) self‑care. This cross‑sectional study investigated the association between sleep quality and self‑care behaviours in 309 patients with chronic heart failure hospitalized in cardiology wards at Imam Khomeini Hospital, Ardabil, Iran, in 2025. Data were collected using the Hippocratic Heart Failure Self-Care Scale (HHFSCS) and the Sleep Quality Scale for Coronary Care Patients (SQ-CC). Poor sleep quality was significantly associated with lower self-care scores ( r = − 0.51, p < 0.001). Hierarchical regression showed that adding sleep quality explained an additional 10.1% of variance in self-care (ΔR² = 0.101, p < 0.001) beyond demographic and clinical factors (overall R² = 0.521). Sleep quality is significantly associated with self-care in heart failure patients. Although the cross-sectional design limits causal inference, these findings suggest that sleep quality may be a modifiable factor worth considering in future interventions designed to improve self-care.

title: Genetic and Molecular Determinants of Cancer Therapy-Related Cardiovascular Toxicity
authors: Paulina Szubińska-Bałaban; Aneta Klotzka; Katarzyna Ziółkowska; Patrycja Marciniak-Stępak; Julia Niedzielska; F Y Russo; Amro Abu Suleiman; Filip Glista; Angelika Kuczmarska; Ewelina Bukowska‐Olech
abstract: Cancer therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity (CTR-CVT) is an umbrella term for myocardial, vascular, electrical, and inflammatory complications of cytotoxic, targeted, immune, and radiation-based therapies. Cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) is used here more narrowly for treatment-related myocardial dysfunction, typically identified by changes in left ventricular ejection fraction, global longitudinal strain, and/or cardiac biomarkers. The pathophysiology of CTR-CVT is multifactorial, but the implicated pathways should not be interpreted as equally causal. The dominant initiating mechanism is therapy-specific - anthracycline injury is best supported by topoisomerase IIβ (TOP2B)-mediated DNA damage with secondary mitochondrial and redox injury; HER2-directed toxicity by disruption of NRG1-ERBB2/ERBB4 survival signalling; fluoropyrimidine toxicity by coronary vasomotor dysfunction; VEGF-pathway inhibition by endothelial dysfunction and hypertension; immune checkpoint inhibitor toxicity by loss of immune tolerance; and radiotherapy injury by endothelial and microvascular damage with progressive fibrosis. Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammation, calcium dysregulation, apoptosis, and ferroptosis frequently act as downstream or amplifying pathways, although the clinical relevance of several regulated cell-death mechanisms remains incompletely established. Genetic susceptibility may further modify risk, but the strength of evidence differs among reported loci. Replicated pharmacogenetic associations, rare variants in established cardiomyopathy genes, and preliminary candidate-gene findings should therefore be considered separately. Most available studies remain limited by small cohorts, heterogeneous phenotyping, ancestry imbalance, and incomplete external replication. This review critically evaluates the hierarchy and strength of mechanistic and genetic evidence and discusses the extent to which these findings can currently inform risk stratification, surveillance, prevention, and treatment in precision cardio-oncology.

title: Association of Serum Anion Gap and Angiographic Severity of Coronary Artery Disease by Gensini Score in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndrome
authors: Muhammad Sohel Rana; Md Abdul Khalaque; Mir Mohammad Arifur Rahman; M Khalequzzaman; Md Abrar Kaiser; Md Shazedur Rahman
journal: Journal of invasive and clinical cardiology.
abstract: Background: The serum anion gap (AG) has been reported to have an association with the severity of coronary artery diseases (CAD). This association is not yet well studied in Bangladesh. Gensini Score (GS) gives insight into the severity of CAD. Acute Coronary Syndrome is a severe type ofcoronary artery disease. The study of severity of CAD by GS in relation to AG following acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains limited in Bangladesh. Methods: This cross-sectional analytical study was conducted at the department of Cardiology, Sir Salimullah Medical College Mitford Hospital, Dhaka, for a duration of 12-months following ethical approval. A total of 90 patients with Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) who underwent coronaryangiography were included after getting written informed consent. 45 patients were included in group A (anion gap 8 mEq/L to 16 mEq/L) and 45 patients were in group B (anion gap >16 mEq/L). Data were collected on pre designed data collection sheet separated case-record form and analyzed by SPSS-26. Results: Mean age of the patients in Group A and Group B was 59.5±11.9 years and 64.9±9.1 years accordingly. Age was significantly higher in Group B than Group A. Among all, 53.3% of the patients had Gensini score ≥50, 46.7% had Gensini score <50. Mean Gensini score in Group A and Group B was 43.9±6.3 and 54.8±1.4 accordingly. Mean Gensini score was significantly higher among the patients with anion gap above 16mEq/L. A cut off value Anion gap>16 mEq/L (AUC=0.899, 95% CI=0.831-0.967, p<0.001) in the prediction of severe CAD (Gensini score ≥50) showed 81.25% sensitivity, 80.95% Specificity, 82.98% PPV, 79.07% NPV and 81.11% accuracy. Conclusion: This study investigated the association of serum anion gap and the severity of coronary artery disease as measured by Gensini Score (GS) in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS). A higher anion gap levels (>16 mEq/L) were associated with increased severity of CAD by Gensini scores in patients with ACS. J Inv Clin Cardiol 2024; 6(2): 65-78

title: Congestive Heart Failure Revealing Takayasu's Disease: About Two Cases at the University Teaching Hospital of Brazzaville
authors: Bakekolo Paterne; Kouala Michel; Mongo Flore; Ngolo Mou-Moué; Kimbally Gibrel; Ellenga Fikahem
abstract: Introduction : Takayasu's disease (TD) is a rare chronic large-vessel vasculitis of unknown etiology that preferentially affects the aorta and its branches. Clinical manifestations are usually dominated by ischemic and vascular signs, and cardiac involvement, although rare, marks an important turning point in the course of the disease.) We report two cases of TD that showed up as congestive heart failure. Case presentations : the first with a four-year history of heart failure previously attributed to hypertensive heart disease, and the second with acute pulmonary edema in the context of a one-year history of intermittent lower-limb claudication. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a dilated cardiomyopathy with severely reduced ejection fraction and moderate aortic and mitral regurgitation in the first patient, and concentric hypertensive heart disease with moderate aortic regurgitation in the second. CT angiography of the aorta and its branches showed arterial wall thickening and occlusive lesions of the supra-aortic and/or iliac arteries in both patients, raising suspicion of TD. The diagnosis was confirmed using the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria, with scores of 6 and 12 points, respectively. Both patients received standard heart failure therapy together with oral corticosteroid therapy. The first patient also received an oral anticoagulant following a transient ischemic stroke and remains on the waiting list for vascular surgery. Clinical signs of heart failure regressed with treatment in both patients. Conclusion: Cardiac involvement can be the presenting feature of Takayasu's disease. This diagnosis should be considered in a young woman presenting with heart failure associated with blood pressure asymmetry or absent peripheral pulses, so as to enable earlier diagnosis and treatment.

title: Application of Patient Journey Mapping in Patients with Cardiovascular Diseases：a scoping review
authors: 王硕
abstract: Purpose. Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of global mortality and disability, and their care spans acute treatment, rehabilitation, and long-term self-management. Patient journey mapping (PJM) is increasingly used to visualise and understand patients' experiences and touchpoints across the care continuum, but its application in CVDs—particularly in stroke—remains fragmented and has not been comprehensively synthesised. This scoping review aims to map the available evidence on PJM among adults with CVDs, describing how journey maps have been defined and developed, where and how they have been applied, what outcomes and barriers have been reported, and where knowledge gaps remain, with a specific focus on stroke survivors. Methods. This review follows the Arksey and O'Malley framework, as refined by Levac et al. and the JBI guidance, and will be reported according to the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework guides eligibility: the population is adults (≥18 years) with established CVDs, defined according to the WHO definition and the GBD 2019 CVD cause list (including coronary heart disease, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, aortic aneurysm, peripheral artery disease, endocarditis, and valvular heart disease); the concept is patient journey mapping and related terms (journey map, patient journey, experience map, service blueprint, touchpoint); and the context is the full hospital–community–home care continuum. Studies focusing on congenital heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, venous thromboembolism, paediatric populations, or risk factors without established CVD will be excluded. We will search PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and Chinese databases (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, SinoMed), supplemented by reference-list screening. Two reviewers will independently screen records and extract data using a piloted charting form. Results will be synthesised through descriptive numerical summaries and thematic synthesis, with a subgroup comparison between stroke and other CVDs. Expected outcomes. This registration pre-specifies the review methods and is expected to produce: (1) a comprehensive map of the volume, geographic and disease distribution of PJM research in CVDs; (2) an overview of the definitions, theoretical frameworks, data sources and participatory approaches used to build journey maps; (3) a description of applications, reported benefits and barriers; and (4) an identification of evidence gaps and priorities for future research, especially for stroke. Search strategies and the data extraction template will be made openly available to support transparency and reuse. Ethical approval is not required because this study uses published literature only.
